messages.content: How should I apply urea to my maize so it is not wasted?

Place it in a band beside the plant rather than broadcasting it across the field.

Urea broadcast on hot dry ground loses a large share to the air before the plant takes it up, so you pay for nitrogen the crop never sees. Placement makes a small quantity work like a larger one.

Split the application: some at planting, then top dress at about three to four weeks. Soil acidity is a separate question and is not what determines whether urea works.
Which fertiliser should I buy for my farm?

I cannot answer that honestly without knowing what your soil is short of, and that is exactly the point.

Buying fertiliser without testing is the most common way smallholders waste money. You end up paying for nutrients the soil already has, while the one nutrient that is actually limiting your yield stays short. The crop does not improve and the fertiliser gets blamed.

What I would suggest:

1. Get a soil test if there is any facility within reach. Your extension officer will know where. The cost is small against a season of the wrong fertiliser.
2. While you wait, improve what does not need a test: organic matter, crop rotation with a legume, and correct placement.
3. When you do apply, place or band fertiliser beside the plant rather than broadcasting it. Broadcast urea on hot dry ground loses a large share to the air before the plant ever sees it.

If testing genuinely is not possible, tell me your crop, your zone and what you grew on that land last season, and I can give you a reasonable starting point.
Why does it matter how I decide about dry season production?

Dry season vegetable production under irrigation usually earns more than the same crop in the wet season, because supply is short and prices are higher, and disease pressure is lower. The constraint is water access and the labour of moving it. Shallow wells, washbores and simple furrow systems are within reach of many smallholders, and drip pays back fastest on high value crops. If what you see in the field does not match this, take a sample to an extension officer rather than guessing.
How is rice grown?

Rice is a staple of West and Central African smallholder systems, known locally as shinkafa (Hausa), iresi (Yoruba). Upland rainfed, lowland or fadama, and fully irrigated. The system dictates variety and water management, so advice that ignores it is useless.
How do I tell striga from fall armyworm on maize?

They look nothing alike once you know where to look.

Striga is a plant. You see a small purple or pink flowered weed growing at the base of the maize, and the maize is yellow and stunted out of proportion to the weed.

Fall armyworm is a caterpillar. You see ragged holes in the young leaves and moist frass packed into the whorl at the centre of the plant.

If the damage is a weed at the base, it is striga. If it is chewing damage in the funnel, it is armyworm.
How do I feed cattle through the dry season?

Dry season feed is the binding constraint on cattle in most of the savanna, and it is a planning problem rather than an emergency. Conserve crop residues at harvest, when they are free and abundant, instead of buying feed at the peak of scarcity. An animal that loses heavy condition in the dry season spends the following wet season regaining it rather than growing. Compare a treated strip against an untreated one, otherwise you cannot tell whether the weather did it.
My soybean is underperforming. Where do I start?

Rows about 50 to 75cm apart with plants close within the row, aiming for a dense even stand that shades out weeds. Harvest as soon as pods are dry and rattling. Leaving it standing invites shattering, and shattered grain on the ground is lost. An excellent break crop before maize. The nitrogen it leaves behind cuts the following season's fertiliser bill. Inoculating seed with rhizobium before planting is a small cost that raises nitrogen fixation and yield, especially on land that has not grown soybean before.
Can you explain that more simply?

Rows about 50 to 75cm apart with plants close within the row, aiming for a dense even stand that shades out weeds. Harvest as soon as pods are dry and rattling. Leaving it standing invites shattering, and shattered grain on the ground is lost. In plain terms, find the source, deal with that, and start with what costs nothing.
Why does it matter how I avoid selling into the harvest glut?

Everyone harvests at the same time and prices fall exactly when your crop is ready. Storing well, so quality holds, or aggregating through a co-operative so you can reach buyers who will not deal in small lots, is usually the largest single price gain available to a smallholder. Selling at the farm gate on the day of harvest is the most expensive habit in smallholder farming.

I want to make and use compost. What should I know?

Composting turns crop residue and household waste into something that feeds the soil rather than just this season's crop. It takes weeks to mature, so start well before you need it rather than when you are about to plant. Turning the heap speeds it up and kills weed seed. Compost is the practical way to build organic matter when bagged fertiliser is out of reach.
Is there any way to deal with armyworm without buying chemicals?

Yes, and on a small plot it is often the better economics.

1. Handpick larvae out of the whorls. Done thoroughly over several days on a small field this genuinely works.
2. Destroy badly damaged plants that will not recover rather than nursing them along.
3. Intercrop so the stand is not a uniform block of maize.
4. Leave the natural enemies alone. Broad sprays kill the wasps and predators that were suppressing the pest for free.
5. After harvest, destroy crop residues, because the pest overwinters in them.

The residue step is the one most farmers skip and it is the one that reduces pressure next season.
Something is wrong with my cassava and I cannot tell what. What should I check?

On cassava a short list of causes covers most of what goes wrong.

What to look for:
- Check for cassava mosaic disease.
- Check for cassava green mite.
- Check for root rot on waterlogged soil.
- Check for late weeding.

Match the symptom to the cause before spending money. The wrong treatment costs cash and loses the window for the right one.
I want to find out what my crop is worth. What should I know?

Prices move week to week and differ between markets, so a number quoted from anywhere other than your own market on the day is unreliable. Traders at the market, other farmers who sold recently, and farmer associations are the practical sources. Check this against what your neighbours are seeing before you act on a whole field.
Why does it matter how I work with the harmattan?

The harmattan brings dry dusty air that speeds drying, which helps a harvested crop and hurts a standing one. Plan drying and storage around it and protect late vegetables from the desiccating wind. Keep a note of what you did and when, because next season that record beats any general advice.
Tell me about growing leafy vegetables.

Leafy vegetables are staples of West and Central African smallholder systems, known locally as ugu / fluted pumpkin, tete / amaranth, ewedu / jute mallow, ila / okra. Leafy types are cut repeatedly at intervals rather than harvested once, so soil fertility must be maintained through the cycle. Short cycle leafy vegetables turn over in weeks, which makes them the practical way to generate cash between long season crops.
I want to start growing cassava. Where do I begin?

Weed control in the first 3 months determines yield more than any other single factor, because cassava canopies late and cannot compete early.

1. Stem cuttings 20 to 25cm long with at least 5 nodes, taken from the middle of mature stems 8 to 12 months old. Never cut from a plant showing mosaic symptoms.
2. Ridges or mounds on heavy or waterlogged soil to prevent root rot. Flat planting is acceptable on free-draining sandy loam.
3. 1m by 1m for sole crop, about 10,000 plants per hectare. Wider at 1m by 1.5m when intercropping with maize.
4. Plant at an angle or upright with two thirds of the cutting buried, buds pointing up.
What is the right way to get tomatoes to market without losses?

Most tomato loss happens between the field and the market, not in the field. Rigid crates instead of raffia baskets sharply reduce bruising, because baskets crush the fruit at the bottom under the weight above. Harvest in the cool of the morning, keep the fruit shaded while it waits, and handle it once rather than repeatedly. Keep a note of what you did and when, because next season that record beats any general advice.

What is the right way to deal with cassava mosaic on cassava?
1. The main control is clean planting material and resistant varieties. Rogue out badly affected plants. There is no spray that cures an infected plant.
What is the best approach to fall armyworm?

Handpicking on small plots, intercropping to break up the stand, encouraging natural enemies, and destroying crop residues after harvest. Damage matters most in early vegetative growth. Late infestation on a tasselled crop rarely justifies treatment cost. Ragged holes and moist sawdust like frass in the whorl. Larvae have an inverted pale Y on the head and four dots in a square on the second to last segment.
Which of those matters most if I can only do one?

Handpicking on small plots, intercropping to break up the stand, encouraging natural enemies, and destroying crop residues after harvest. Damage matters most in early vegetative growth. Late infestation on a tasselled crop rarely justifies treatment cost. The unpaid work usually beats the bought input: clean planting material, correct spacing, and weeding on time.
How do I sell through a cooperative?

Selling as a group opens buyers who will not deal in small quantities, and spreads the cost of transport, storage and testing across members. It also gives some negotiating position, which an individual smallholder arriving alone at a market does not have. The gain is usually larger than any agronomic change available in the same season. Keep a note of what you did and when, because next season that record beats any general advice.
My tomato plants are wilting but the leaves are still green. What should I spray?

Before you buy anything, do a simple test, because if this is what I suspect then no spray will help and you would be spending money for nothing.

Cut a wilting stem near the base and suspend the cut end in a clear glass of water. Watch for a minute or two. If a milky white thread streams down from the cut into the water, that is bacterial wilt.

Wilting while the leaves stay green is the classic sign. There is no chemical cure for it. What you can do:

1. Remove affected plants along with the soil around the roots, and do not compost them.
2. Rotate away from tomato, pepper and other related crops on that ground for several seasons.
3. Improve drainage, because the bacterium moves in wet soil.

If the milky ooze does not appear, then look at root damage, nematodes or simple water stress instead, and tell me what you find.
Is fall armyworm the same as the armyworm that moves in swarms?

They are different pests with similar names, and the control differs.

**Fall armyworm** stays with the crop it hatched on. It feeds inside the maize whorl, is present in the field more or less continuously once established, and is the one that leaves frass in the funnel.

**African armyworm** moves in large migrating groups, strips foliage from cereals and pasture, and appears suddenly in outbreaks after certain rainfall patterns. It feeds openly on the leaves rather than hiding in the whorl.

If the damage is inside the funnel with frass, treat it as fall armyworm. If large numbers appeared overnight and are eating leaves in the open, report it, because outbreaks are managed at district level and your extension service will want to know.
When is the best time to sell my maize?

Prices are lowest right at harvest, when everyone sells at once, so selling at the farm gate on harvest day is usually the most expensive habit in smallholder farming.

If you can dry properly and store well so quality holds, or sell through a co-operative that aggregates enough volume to reach larger buyers, that is normally where the gain is.

I cannot tell you today's price. That moves week to week and by market, so ask traders there or a local farmers' association.
What do I need to get right when planting maize?

Moisture stress at tasselling and silking causes the largest yield loss of any stage.

1. 75cm between rows and 25cm within rows, one plant per stand, about 53,000 plants per hectare.
2. Split nitrogen: a basal compound fertiliser at planting, then top dress with urea at about 3 to 4 weeks, and again at knee height on poor soils. Place fertiliser in a band beside the plant, not broadcast, to cut losses.

If what you see in the field does not match this, take a sample to an extension officer rather than guessing.
Can you help me write a business plan for a barbing salon?

That is outside what I do. I only cover farming: crops, livestock, soils, storage and getting produce to market.

If your plan involves an agricultural enterprise, poultry, fish, vegetables for market, then I can help with the farming side of it, though not the finances.
My yam is underperforming. Where do I start?

Seed yam of about 250 to 300g, or setts produced by the minisett technique, which multiplies planting material from a single tuber. Large mounds or ridges for drainage and tuber expansion. Compacted soil produces short, forked tubers. Milk harvest of the first tuber can be taken while the plant continues, or a single harvest at senescence. Cure tubers in shade before storing in a ventilated barn. Damaged tubers rot and spread rot to the rest.
Can you explain that more simply?

Seed yam of about 250 to 300g, or setts produced by the minisett technique, which multiplies planting material from a single tuber. Large mounds or ridges for drainage and tuber expansion. Compacted soil produces short, forked tubers. The short version is to treat what is causing it rather than what you can see.
How much water does rice need?

It depends entirely on which system you are growing in, and that is not me avoiding the question. The answer genuinely changes.

Which are you?

1. Upland rainfed, grown on ordinary sloping or flat land and depending on rain alone.
2. Lowland or fadama, in a low lying area that naturally holds water.
3. Fully irrigated with a controlled supply.

If you are lowland or irrigated, the practical guidance is to keep a shallow standing depth through tillering, and then drain the field before harvest so the ground firms up enough to work on. Continuous deep flooding is not better and wastes water.

If you are upland, you are managing rainfall rather than water depth, and your priorities move to weed control and choosing a variety suited to upland conditions. Tell me which one you are and I will be more specific.
Wetin dey chop my maize leaf? I see white worm for inside the middle.

Na fall armyworm. Na the caterpillar dey stay for inside the whorl, the middle of the plant, and na there e dey chop.

How you go know say na am:

1. Open the middle of some plant for morning or evening time, when dem dey active.
2. The caterpillar head get white mark like Y wey turn upside down.
3. Near the tail, you go see four black dot wey stand like square.

If the farm small, pick dem comot with hand for some days. E dey work well. After harvest, clear the stalks and plough them in, or destroy them as your local guidance advises, na there dem dey hide reach next season.

If you go spray, use product wey dem register for fall armyworm for maize, follow the rate wey dey for label, and pour am enter the middle. Spray wey you pour on top leaf no go reach the caterpillar.
What is the market price of maize in Kano this week?

I do not know, and I will not guess at it. Prices move week to week and by market, and a number invented by me could cost you real money at the point of sale.

For a current price, ask traders at the market itself, other farmers who sold recently, or a local farmers' association, which often tracks it.

What I can say generally is that prices are at their lowest right at harvest when everyone sells at once. If you can dry properly and store well, or sell through a cooperative that aggregates, that is usually where the gain is.
How do I tell cassava mosaic apart from other problems on cassava?

Cassava mosaic on cassava can be identified in the field before you treat.

What to look for:
- Yellow and green mottling, distorted and reduced leaves, stunted plants.

Carried by whitefly and, most importantly, by planting infected stem cuttings. The main control is clean planting material and resistant varieties. Rogue out badly affected plants. There is no spray that cures an infected plant.

Yes, and on a small plot it is often the better economics.

1. Handpick larvae out of the whorls. Done thoroughly over several days on a small field this genuinely works.
2. Destroy badly damaged plants that will not recover rather than nursing them along.
3. Intercrop so the stand is not a uniform block of maize.
4. Leave the natural enemies alone. Broad sprays kill the wasps and predators that were suppressing the pest for free.
5. After harvest, destroy crop residues, because the pest overwinters in them.

The residue step is the one most farmers skip and it is the one that reduces pressure next season.
Can I mix two pesticides together to save time?

Do not do that on my say-so. Some combinations are unsafe or destroy each other's effect, and this varies by product.

Check both labels for what they say about tank mixing, and ask your extension officer before combining anything.
When is it actually fall armyworm?

Only when the damage is in the whorl. Ragged holes across the young leaves as they unfurl, and moist frass packed into the funnel at the centre of the plant.

If it is a weed at the base, that is striga. If the holes are in the stem with dry frass, that is a borer. If it is fine pale streaks along the leaf, that is maize streak virus.

Armyworm is common, but it is not the answer to every maize problem, and treating the wrong one wastes the money and the window.
Stop asking questions and just give me your best guess.

I would rather ask one question than guess wrong and cost you money on the wrong treatment.

Tell me the crop and what you can see on the plant, and I will give you a straight answer.

What goes wrong when farmers do not stock a catfish pond?

Stocking rate and water quality are one decision, not two. Overstocking raises ammonia, stresses the fish and stunts growth no matter how well you feed. Fish gulping at the surface is a warning that the water cannot carry the load. Either exchange water more often or reduce the number of fish; feeding harder into bad water only makes it worse.
I have half a hectare and almost no money this season. What is the single best thing I can do for my maize?

Weed on time. If you can only do one thing, that is the one.

Weeding costs labour rather than cash, and on a small maize plot it changes yield more than any input you could buy with the money you do not have. Maize is most vulnerable to competition in its first few weeks, so weeding early matters far more than weeding often.

After that, in order of how much they give back per naira spent:

1. Correct spacing and one plant per stand, which costs nothing but attention at planting.
2. Planting on established rains rather than the first shower, which avoids a replant.
3. If any cash exists, a small amount of nitrogen placed beside the plant at about three to four weeks, rather than broadcast. Placement makes a small quantity work like a larger one.

Avoid spending scarce money on spraying unless you have actually scouted and found a problem worth treating.
What is eating the middle of my maize? There is a wet powder like sawdust in there.

That wet sawdust is frass, the caterpillar's droppings, and packed in the whorl it points squarely at fall armyworm.

Confirm before you spend anything:

- Open the whorl on several plants across the field, early morning or late evening when the larvae are active.
- Look for a pale upside-down Y marking on the head.
- Look for four dark dots in a square near the tail end.

Count how many plants in twenty are affected. That number, not the presence of a single caterpillar, decides whether treatment is worth the cost.
My cassava is underperforming. Where do I start?

Weed control in the first 3 months determines yield more than any other single factor, because cassava canopies late and cannot compete early. 1m by 1m for sole crop, about 10,000 plants per hectare. Wider at 1m by 1.5m when intercropping with maize. Improved varieties such as TME 419, TMS 30572 and TMS 98/0505 offer mosaic resistance and higher root yield than most local landraces. Stem cuttings 20 to 25cm long with at least 5 nodes, taken from the middle of mature stems 8 to 12 months old. Never cut from a plant showing mosaic symptoms.
Can you explain that more simply?

Ridges or mounds on heavy or waterlogged soil to prevent root rot. Flat planting is acceptable on free-draining sandy loam. 9 to 12 months for early varieties, up to 18 months for late. Roots left too long become woody and lose starch quality. In plain terms, find the source, deal with that, and start with what costs nothing.
There is a small purple flowered weed growing near my maize stems and the maize is yellow and stunted. What is it?

That is striga, also called witchweed. A flowering weed at the base of the stem is not an insect problem, so do not treat it as armyworm.

Striga attaches to the maize root and draws from it, which is why the maize yellows far more than the small weed above ground would explain. It thrives where nitrogen and organic matter are depleted, so it is a soil fertility problem wearing a weed's clothing.

Pull it before it flowers. Each plant that flowers sheds very many long-lived seeds.

Walk me through planting oil palm on a small plot.

1. About 9m triangular spacing, roughly 143 palms per hectare. Crowded palms shade each other and yield falls.
2. Plant tenera hybrid seedlings from a reputable source. Dura palms grown from random seed give much thicker shells and less oil.

That is outside what I do. I only cover farming: crops, livestock, soils, storage and getting produce to market.

If you have a farm question I am glad to help with that.
When should I plant soybean?

Plant on established rains, not on the first shower, in every zone. A false start is the most expensive common mistake. Harvest as soon as pods are dry and rattling. Leaving it standing invites shattering, and shattered grain on the ground is lost. Conditions differ between zones and soils, so treat this as a starting point.
How do I control cocoa black pod?
1. Harvest frequently, remove and bury or destroy infected pods, prune for an open canopy and improve drainage. Sanitation does most of the work.
I want to use cover crops between seasons. What should I know?

A cover crop over the off season protects the soil surface, adds organic matter and smothers weeds before they seed. Bare ground between seasons is a loss you do not see until yields drift down over several years. A legume cover adds nitrogen as well, which makes it close to free. Keep a note of what you did and when, because next season that record beats any general advice.
What is the right way to goat worms?

Worm burden rises in the wet season when larvae survive on pasture. Pale gums and poor condition despite adequate feed suggest a heavy burden. Rotate products rather than using the same one every time, because repeating one breeds resistance, and ask locally which still works. Ask the older farmers in your area what has worked there, since local experience beats a general rule.
How do I deal with striga on my maize, sorghum, millet, upland rice?

Rotation with legumes, restoring soil fertility and organic matter, hand pulling before the weed flowers and seeds, and resistant varieties where available. Small purple or pink flowered weed emerging near cereal stems, with the crop stunted and yellowed out of proportion to the visible weed. A striga problem is a soil fertility problem. It thrives where nitrogen and organic matter are depleted.
Is it too late in the season to do that now?

Rotation with legumes, restoring soil fertility and organic matter, hand pulling before the weed flowers and seeds, and resistant varieties where available. Small purple or pink flowered weed emerging near cereal stems, with the crop stunted and yellowed out of proportion to the visible weed. Field changes are rarely visible in days. Leave an untreated strip so you have something to compare against.

If your plan involves an agricultural enterprise, poultry, fish, vegetables for market, then I can help with the farming side of it, though not the finances.
What actually works against quelea and birds?
1. Scaring must be sustained through the vulnerable window from grain fill to harvest. Community wide timing works far better than one farmer acting alone, because birds simply move next door.

What is the right way to cattle down?

A cow that has been down for more than a day is an emergency, not a management question. Causes range from metabolic to injury to infectious, and telling them apart needs hands on the animal. Call a veterinary officer rather than treating blind.
What actually works against tuta absoluta?
1. Exclusion netting over nurseries, pheromone traps for monitoring and mass trapping, removal and destruction of affected material, and rotation away from tomato and related crops.

My chickens are dying suddenly. Many died in two days. Some have twisted necks.

Sudden high mortality with twisted necks and nervous signs points strongly to Newcastle disease. Act today, because it moves fast through a flock.

What to do now:

1. Separate the birds still looking healthy from the sick ones immediately, and handle the healthy group first each time you go in.
2. Stop all movement of birds in or out. Do not sell or give away birds from this flock, and do not bring replacements in yet.
3. Dispose of dead birds by burying or burning them. Do not leave carcasses where other birds or animals reach them.
4. Contact your veterinary or extension officer today so the outbreak is known about locally.

There is no treatment that cures Newcastle once a flock breaks with it. Vaccination is the only real control, and it has to be in place before an outbreak, on schedule. Once you have restocked, keep the vaccination programme up, quarantine every new or returning bird before mixing, and never bring unsold birds back from the market straight into the flock.

Why does it matter how I store grain without chemicals?

Hermetic bags such as PICS control storage insects without chemicals, by sealing the grain so the insects inside consume the oxygen and die. They work extremely well, but only if the inner liner is sealed properly every single time it is opened. A bag left loosely closed is just an ordinary bag, and this is the step farmers skip.
Why does it matter how I goat worms?

Worm burden rises in the wet season when larvae survive on pasture. Pale gums and poor condition despite adequate feed suggest a heavy burden. Rotate products rather than using the same one every time, because repeating one breeds resistance, and ask locally which still works.
How do I deworm my small ruminants?

Worm burden rises sharply in the wet season when larvae survive on pasture, so timing matters more than which product you use. Deworming on a fixed schedule with the same product year after year breeds resistance. Ask your veterinary or extension officer what is working locally, and rotate products rather than repeating one. Compare a treated strip against an untreated one, otherwise you cannot tell whether the weather did it.
My crop is dying. What do I do?

I can help, but I need a little more to go on, because the right action differs completely depending on the answer.

Tell me:

1. Which crop, and roughly how old is it?
2. What exactly do you see? Yellowing, wilting, holes in leaves, spots, or the plant simply not growing?
3. Is it spread evenly across the field, or in patches?
4. Has it been unusually wet or dry recently?

That last one matters more than people expect. Patches rather than even spread usually points to soil or a soil borne disease, while even spread across the whole field more often points to weather, nutrition or something applied. Give me those details and I can narrow it down.
My goat has a fever, runny nose and sores in the mouth. Several others look sick too.

Fever with nasal discharge, mouth sores and rapid spread through a flock points at peste des petits ruminants. Act today, because it moves quickly and kills young stock hardest.

What to do now:

1. Separate visibly sick animals from the rest and handle the healthy ones first each time you go in.
2. Stop all movement in or out. Do not sell, lend or buy animals while this is running.
3. Contact your veterinary or extension officer today so the outbreak is known locally.
4. Do not leave carcasses out. Your veterinary or extension officer will tell you the correct disposal method for your area.

Vaccination is the real control and it has to be in place beforehand. Once you have restocked, keep it up and quarantine every newly bought animal before it joins the flock.
Any advice on how to start beekeeping?

Site hives away from paths, livestock and homes, with shade and water within reach, because bees that must fly far for water work less and defend more. Harvest leaves enough honey for the colony to hold through the dearth period, and a colony stripped bare will abscond. Beekeeping fits well beside cropping, since the same bees improve pollination on nearby fields.
My cassava leaves are yellow and twisted. I sprayed insecticide twice and nothing changed. What stronger chemical should I use?

Please stop spending money on spray for this. Yellow mottled and twisted cassava leaves are cassava mosaic disease, and no insecticide, at any strength, will reverse it.

It is a virus. It is carried by whitefly, but far more importantly it is carried in the stem cuttings themselves. If you planted cuttings taken from an infected plant, the crop was infected before it ever came up, which is why spraying changed nothing.

What to do:

1. Accept this season's crop for what it is. Rogue out the worst affected plants.
2. This is the important one: never take planting material from a plant showing these symptoms. Take cuttings only from healthy vigorous plants, from the middle of stems eight to twelve months old.
3. Get improved resistant varieties if you can. TME 419 and TMS 30572 are widely grown for this reason.

Clean planting material is the whole control. Farmers who fix that one habit stop having this problem.
